newsitem.title: USA: Congress mulls law on homeowner mortgage insurance.
newsitem.headline: Congress mulls law on homeowner mortgage insurance.

text.p: Some lawmakers on Capitol Hill are trying to push through legislation that would bar lenders from requiring homeowners to pay mortgage insurance once they build up a certain amount of equity in their homes.

The House Banking Committee overwhelmingly approved such a provision late Thursday. A bi-partisan group of senators is backing a related measure, but a committee vote on the proposed bill was postponed earlier this week after panel members failed to agree in time on key details.
Senate aides said a vote could be scheduled for sometime in April after Congress returns from a spring recess, but no date has been set.
Consumer groups have hailed the efforts to pass legislation, saying changes could help save consumers hundreds of dollars a year in unnecessary insurance premiums.

The savings have been estimated to range from $300 to more than $900 a year. A homeowner making a 10 percent downpayment and taking out a $100,000 30-year loan, for example, would no longer have to pay mortgage insurance after 12 years of regular payments, according to some estimates.

"Many homeowners have been allowed to continue ... payments after their equity stake in their home would indicate that such insurance to protect the investor against default was no longer necessary," House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach, an Iowa Republican, said earlier this week.
Many lenders and insurers have voiced support for the overall thrust of legislation, but have expressed concern about some of its specifics.

Private mortgage insurance, designed to protect lenders from potential loan defaults, is usually required by lenders when a homebuyer makes a downpayment of less than 20 percent and borrows the rest. Homeowners pay the premiums as part of their monthly mortgage payments.

"Homeowners that can only afford a low downpayment initially shouldn't be treated like second-class borrowers once they've built up the equity that would have let them avoid the mortgage insurance costs altogether if paid up front," said Michelle Meier of the Consumers Union.

The House bill, approved by a 36-1 panel vote, would require lenders to cancel private mortgage insurance requirements once a borrower's equity stake has reached at least 25 percent of the original value of the house, if the borrower is also current on mortgage payments.

But the cancellation requirement only applies to loans which originate after the bill becomes law, a provision supported by some industry groups that had been concerned about the prospects of a retroactive requirement.
The bill would also give homeowners the right to cancel insurance if they have met the conditions of the most recent notice provided to them regarding their insurance.

Some lenders no longer require homeowners to carry mortgage insurance once they build up a 20 percent equity stake in their homes, but many homeowners are unaware that they have the right to cancel their insurance.
What's more, some lenders use boilerplate contract clauses that require homeowners to pay mortgage insurance for the entire life of their 30-year mortgages. The bill also takes aim at that practice.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato of New York is sponsoring legislation that would force lenders to cancel mortgage insurance for future homeowners once they build up a 20 percent equity stake in their homes.
It would give current homeowners the right to cancel once they reach the 20 percent threshold and would require written notification at least once a year.

But some senators on the panel disagree on whether to require notification or automatic cancellaton and some are uncertain about who, if anybody, at the federal level would monitor the new requirements.
Nevada Democrat Richard Bryan, a co-sponsor of the Senate bill, wants the banking panel to take up the matter again as soon as possible.
"Every homeowner in America who pays private mortgage insurance should be outraged that this legislation is not moving quickly through Congress," Bryan said after the vote was canceled.
